idiom_name: right-size the storage once growth has ended (realloc to the live length, or swap/copy into an exactly-sized container)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: keep the size/capacity split visible - a growable buffer plus a length - and, when the growth phase ends, replace the oversized storage with storage sized to the live range: realloc the block to the live length, or build an exactly-sized copy and swap or drop the original. The contract has three obligations: run it at a quiescent point, because the operation may move the storage and every iterator, pointer or view into it becomes invalid; do not rely on it for a hard bound, because most realizations are requests the allocator may decline; and expect the copy-based forms to need a second allocation of the same magnitude, so never inside a growth loop. Where a runtime owns capacity - a garbage collector, an arena, a pool - the trim is that runtime's job or the arena's, and the correct move is to rebuild the value and drop the old reference rather than to try to shrink in place.
code_sketch:
trim(container):                              # once growth has ended, no live views
    exact = right_sized_copy_of(container)    # storage == live range
    swap(exact, container)                    # old storage released here
    # allocator-owned variant: realloc(buf, len * elem_size)
    # request-only variant:    container.shrink_to_fit()   (may be ignored)
pitfalls: Trimming inside the growth loop instead of after it: every append then reallocates, so amortized O(1) growth becomes repeated O(n) copies.
Reading or writing through a pointer, iterator, view or buffer export taken before the trim - the storage may have moved or been replaced.
Treating a non-binding request, or a rebuild whose old object is still referenced, as released memory.

Wrong move: shrinking a Go slice with a reslice like s = s[:n] -> cap stays the same and the small view keeps the whole peak backing array reachable, which is the opposite of the intent -> instead copy into right-sized storage, s = append(make([]T, 0, len(s)), s...), the only form the Go blog and SliceTricks wiki treat as releasing the old array.

Wrong move: calling .NET TrimExcess on a collection at 95% fill and booking the memory as freed -> it deliberately does nothing when Count is 90% or more of Capacity, so capacity silently stays at the peak -> instead read Count/Capacity before and after, and accept the slack when utilization is high.

Wrong move: using basic_string::reserve(0) or a shrinking reserve as a portable C++ trim -> C++17 standardized reserve to never shrink (LWG P0966), so the string keeps its capacity while the code assumes it released -> instead call shrink_to_fit where it is honored, or force the release with the swap-with-exact-copy idiom.
